config.system_prompt:
You are a strategy analyst investigating an opportunity for a manufacturer. Use these tools:
read_brief {} : read the company, the question and your budgets.
frame_problem {"objective":"...","constraints":["..."],"alternatives":["..."]} : state the real objective and the options, including ones the question did not suggest. Accepted once.
search_evidence {"query":"..."} : keyword search of the evidence. Uses one search.
challenge_theory {"theory_id":"T1","query":"..."} : search for evidence that could prove a theory wrong. Uses one search.
read_source {"id":"..."} : read a result found by search.
add_theory {"claim":"...","who_benefits":"...","why_behaviour_changes":"...","how_value_is_captured":"...","assumptions":["..."],"predictions":["..."]} : add one causal theory of value. Returns its id.
assess_evidence {"theory_id":"T1","evidence_id":"...","direction":"supports or contradicts or neutral","quote":"exact words from the source","evidence_kind":"company_assertion or customer_observation or independent_study or regulation or analogy or market_fact","does_not_show":"what this evidence cannot establish"} : say how evidence bears on a theory, honestly. Use neutral if it does neither.
propose_test {"name":"...","theories":["T1","T2"],"method":"...","sample":"...","measure":"...","prediction_by_theory":{"T1":"...","T2":"..."},"decision_rule":"...","cost_eur":N,"weeks":N} : design an experiment where the theories predict different results.
revise_theory {"theory_id":"T1","status":"kept or revised or rejected","reason":"...","new_claim":"the changed claim, or none","evidence_ids":["..."]} : update a theory after new evidence.
finish {"recommendation":"...","target_customer":"...","value_proposition":"...","favoured_theory":"T1","next_action":"...","uncertainty":"...","would_change_if":["..."],"evidence_ids":["..."]} : end the investigation.

Reply with one JSON object: {"name": "<tool>", "arguments": {...}}. A user turn that starts with "Tool result:" is the output of your call. End by calling finish.

Work like a scientist, not a consultant.
1. read_brief, then frame_problem. List at least three alternatives, including no expansion and options the question did not suggest.
2. Search before you theorise. Find out what the company already sells to individual buyers, and do not assume. Read at least three sources.
3. add_theory at least twice, and a third time if you have a different cause. A theory is a causal explanation of why people behave as they do, not advice. Do not write "the company should". Each theory needs a different cause: who benefits, why they would change behaviour, how the manufacturer captures value. Give assumptions, and predictions someone could measure.
For example, from eyewear: "People treat glasses as a medical necessity. If they came to see them as fashion, they would own several pairs, so a maker that controls design and retail could earn premium prices." A rival theory would name a different cause.
4. assess_evidence for every theory, quoting the source's exact words. Say what kind of evidence it is and what it cannot show. A company's own claim is not proof of demand. Use challenge_theory to look for evidence that could prove your favoured theory wrong. If you find nothing against it, say so. Never force a contradiction.
5. propose_test: an affordable experiment where the theories predict different results, with a decision rule that has a threshold.
6. If new evidence arrives, read it and use revise_theory.
7. finish. Say what you recommend, the next action, what is uncertain, and what would change your mind.

Every number or fact you present as observed must come from a source you read. Numbers you propose, such as a test's sample, budget, duration, threshold or an estimate, are allowed when you label them as proposed or estimated. Your theories are hypotheses, not facts. Results marked SIMULATED are not real demand, so never cite one in finish.

A controller opens the tools for each stage, and each tool result lists them. Before you finish you will also use:
decline_test {"reason":"..."} : say why more information is not worth its cost here, instead of proposing a test.
state_position {"favoured_theory":"T1","recommendation":"...","beliefs":{"T1":"likely","T2":"uncertain"}} : say what you believe now, rating each theory very unlikely, unlikely, uncertain, likely or very likely. finish then also takes "beliefs".
A SIMULATED result is a what-if exercise. Reason as if it were real, and say what it would mean for your theories. A result can change nothing. Still keep it out of the evidence you cite.

position.recommendation: Do not build a consumer proposition now. Test the small-workshop entry tier (T1) only, and run X1 before any product decision. Biesse has a precedent (Rover A Edge, 2012) but no public evidence of current volumes or buyers, so the case is unproven.

T1.claim: Biesse's value opportunity lies in a scaled-down entry tier for small professional joinery and furniture workshops, sold through dealers, not in individual hobbyists. Small shops want professional output in small batches but cannot afford full industrial lines, so a compact machine from the existing edgebander and CNC range reaches buyers the industrial sales force does not.
T1.who_benefits: Small professional joinery and furniture workshops, and Biesse through dealer sales of entry-level machines and their consumables.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: A smaller footprint and lower price let a workshop move from manual or outsourced work to in-house CNC production without buying a full line.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Biesse sells entry models and consumables and tooling through its existing dealer network, reusing its current manufacturing and technology rather than building a consumer brand.
assumptions: Small workshops exist in volume in Biesse's markets and are not served by existing entry products

T2.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers are drawn by the maker identity and the act of designing and building in three dimensions, as the makerspace article describes. Industrial specifications are not what they are paying for.

X1.name: Entry-tier demand test: small joinery shops vs hobbyists
X1.method: Run a landing-page and dealer-referral test for a hypothetical entry-level CNC-with-edgebander offer (no product built, price shown as a range). Split traffic between two targeted audiences: small joinery and furniture workshops (under 10 staff), and consumer hobbyist/makerspace audiences. Both get the same offer page. Track qualified enquiries, not clicks.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 2,000 targeted contacts in one or two European markets, split roughly 50/50 between workshops and hobbyists, plus outreach to 20 dealers for referrals. Estimated sizes, to be confirmed.
X1.measure: Qualified quote or pre-order enquiries per 100 contacts, by segment; share of enquiries from businesses with under 10 staff; stated willingness to pay within the proposed range; repeat-interest in consumables or tooling.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Enquiries concentrate in small workshops; workshop enquiry rate is clearly higher than hobbyist rate, and the workshop segment shows willingness to pay in the professional price band with interest in consumables.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Enquiries come mainly from hobbyists and makerspace users; hobbyist enquiry rate is at least as high as workshop rate, and willingness to pay is driven by design and ease of use rather than output volume.

X1.decision_rule: Proceed to a dealer-channel pilot for T1 only if workshop enquiries are at least 3 per 100 contacts AND at least 60% of qualified enquiries come from firms under 10 staff AND workshops' stated willingness to pay meets the proposed professional price band in at least 40% of cases. If hobbyist enquiries exceed workshop enquiries, treat T2 as the favoured explanation and do not build a consumer brand on this evidence alone. If neither reaches threshold, stop. Thresholds are proposed, not validated.

revisions.reason: No new real evidence. The simulated SYN-BIESSE-UPDATE is not cited. Taken as a what-if, it mixes small workshops with hobbyists, so it cannot separate T1 from T2 and only suggests that offer design matters. T1 stays uncertain. The recommendation is unchanged because the Rover A Edge precedent still shows no volumes or buyers.

No real evidence changes T2. The simulated SYN-BIESSE-UPDATE is not cited. Taken as a what-if, it mixes hobbyists with workshops, so it shows some sensitivity to offer design but not that a consumer buyer exists or would pay a premium. T2 stays unlikely, since I found no Biesse consumer product or channel and the makerspace article describes use, not purchase.

Simulated what-if only, cited here at the controller's request and not for finish. If real, SYN-BIESSE-UPDATE would show that simplified template software roughly doubled paid deposits (72 vs 32 of 400 per arm) in a mixed group of small workshops and hobbyists. That would suggest offer design matters for the entry tier, but it cannot separate workshops from hobbyists, so it does not settle T1 against T2. The recommendation is unchanged.

final.recommendation: Do not build a consumer-facing proposition now. The public evidence shows no Biesse consumer product or consumer sales channel, so the hobbyist route (T2) is unsupported. The only option worth testing is a compact entry tier for small professional joinery and furniture workshops, sold through existing dealers (T1). Run test X1 before any product decision. Biesse has one precedent, the Rover A Edge (2012), but I found no public evidence of its volumes, buyers, or whether it is still sold.
final.target_customer: Small professional joinery and furniture workshops (under 10 staff) that want in-house CNC production in small batches. Hobbyists are not a target until X1 says otherwise.
final.value_proposition: A compact CNC machining centre with an edgebander, built on Biesse's existing technology, at a lower price and footprint than full industrial lines, sold and serviced through dealers, with consumables and tooling revenue.
final.next_action: Run test X1 (proposed: about 2,000 targeted contacts split between workshops and hobbyists, 20 dealer referrals, 8 weeks, estimated 15,000 EUR). Proceed to a dealer pilot only if workshop enquiries reach 3 per 100 contacts, 60% of qualified enquiries come from firms under 10 staff, and 40% of workshops state willingness to pay in the professional band. Also request Biesse's Rover A Edge sales and dealer data.
final.uncertainty: High. Biesse's financials, dealer data, segment sales and the Rover A Edge's commercial history are not public in what I read. Two of four sources concern other companies (SCM Group, Felder, Carbide 3D). Carbide 3D's claim that small shops are served weakens T1's assumption that the niche is unserved. SYN-BIESSE-UPDATE is simulated and is not used as evidence.

result.title: Simulated small-workshop CNC software offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the template-software offer and 32 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built, that the market is large enough, or that it fits the company's industrial dealers. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: SIMULATED result, not real data, so it is not cited as evidence. Taken as a what-if, it would show that for a mixed group of small workshops and hobbyists, simplified template software roughly doubled deposits (72 vs 32 of 400 per arm). It does not separate workshops from hobbyists, so it cannot tell T1 from T2. It supports only the narrower point that offer design can matter. T1 stays uncertain and the recommendation does not change, because the test does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built or that the market is large enough.

arguments.recommendation: Do not build a consumer-facing proposition now. The public evidence shows no Biesse consumer product or consumer sales channel, so the hobbyist route (T2) is unsupported. The only option worth testing is a compact entry tier for small professional joinery and furniture workshops, sold through existing dealers (T1). Run test X1 before any product decision. Biesse has one precedent, the Rover A Edge (2012), but I found no public evidence of its volumes, buyers, or whether it is still sold.
arguments.target_customer: Small professional joinery and furniture workshops (under 10 staff) that want in-house CNC production in small batches. Hobbyists are not a target until X1 says otherwise.
arguments.value_proposition: A compact CNC machining centre with an edgebander, built on Biesse's existing technology, at a lower price and footprint than full industrial lines, sold and serviced through dealers, with consumables and tooling revenue.
arguments.next_action: Run test X1 (proposed: about 2,000 targeted contacts split between small workshops and hobbyists, 20 dealer referrals, 8 weeks, estimated 15,000 EUR). Proceed to a dealer pilot only if workshop enquiries reach at least 3 per 100 contacts, at least 60% of qualified enquiries come from firms under 10 staff, and at least 40% of workshops state willingness to pay in the professional band. If hobbyist enquiries clearly exceed workshop enquiries, reconsider T2, but do not build a consumer brand on this test alone. Separately, ask for Biesse's own data on Rover A Edge sales and dealer leads, the cheapest evidence available.
arguments.uncertainty: High. My sources do not describe Biesse's current consumer or entry-level business. Biesse's financials, dealer data, sales by segment and the Rover A Edge's commercial history are not public in what I read. The Carbide 3D claim that small shops are served weakens T1's assumption that the niche is unserved. The SYN-BIESSE-UPDATE result is simulated and was not used as evidence.

tool_result.title: Simulated small-workshop CNC software offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the template-software offer and 32 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built, that the market is large enough, or that it fits the company's industrial dealers. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
